messages.subject: event charts in ggplot2?
parts:
Has anyone here done anything with event charts in ggplot2? I've used
the Hmisc function "event.chart" (simple output shown at

I'll follow-up if I write anything similar using the ggplot package.

Thanks,
Erik

messages.subject: Re: event charts in ggplot2?
parts:
Hi Erik,

I don't know the exact code which you could use to do this, but I
would check out either the path geom or the histogram geom and use
coord_flip() to turn the graph sideways. It seems like there should be
a number of ways to do this. You could also group the observations by
whether they survived, were censored, etc. and then use this status to
group by using geom_path(aes(x,y,shape = group),data = x) in order to
get different symbols for the different endpoints. Just a thought. I
would look through the book to put together the exact code.

Ben

messages.author: 0c39e60ddb38622b
messages.subject: Re: event charts in ggplot2?
parts:
Hi Erik:

Here's a basic version - feel free to improve it.

d <- structure(list(patient = 1:10, start = c(0, 1, 2, 4, 4, 0, 2,
2, 4, 3), end = c(11, 13, 7, 13, 10, 11, 5, 13, 10, 10), event = structure(c(1L,
3L, 1L, 3L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 3L, 1L, 1L), .Label = c("death", "dropout",
"survived"), class = "factor")), .Names = c("patient", "start",
"end", "event"), row.names = c(NA, -10L), class = "data.frame")

p <- ggplot(d, aes(x = patient))
p + geom_point(aes(y = start), shape = 1) + geom_point(aes(y = end, shape = event), size = 3) +
     geom_linerange(aes(ymin = start, ymax = end)) + coord_flip()

I increased the size of the end event shapes to enhance visibility of a patient's outcome.

HTH,
Dennis

messages.author: 1c4479e879526ead
messages.subject: Re: event charts in ggplot2?
parts:
Thank you Dennis, that looks good. I had already started my
own implementation by the time I read this, and ended up with
the following. It takes a data.frame, and a vector of variable
names that indicate *dates* you'd like to plot. As for now, it
uses dates, but that could easily be extended to relative days.

It also lets you include an arbitrary number of "event.vars" to
mark on the figure, by using the melt function from the reshape
package.

It also lets you sample a portion of cases for large data.frames,
and lets you sort the y-axis by a date, such as enrollment date.

Reproducible example below:

library(ggplot2)

## test data
df.test <- data.frame(study.entry.date = sample(seq(as.Date("1990-01-01"),
as.Date("2005-01-01"), by = 1), 500, replace =
TRUE))
df.test <- transform(df.test, first.sae.date = study.entry.date +
sample(1:500,
500, replace = TRUE),
last.visit.date = study.entry.date +
sample(500:2000, 500,
replace = TRUE))

## basic implementation
gg.event.chart <- function(data, event.vars, order.var, sample.n) {
if(!missing(sample.n))
data <- data[sample(1:nrow(data), sample.n), ]

if(!missing(order.var))
data <- data[order(data[[order.var]]),]

data$.n <- 1:nrow(data)
data <- data[c(".n", event.vars)]
mdf <- melt(data, id.vars = ".n")

ggplot(data = data, aes_string(x = tail(event.vars, 1), y = ".n")) +
geom_segment(aes_string(xend = event.vars[1], yend = ".n")) +
scale_x_date() + geom_point(aes_string(x = "value",
colour = "variable"),
data = mdf)
}

## produce the figure
gg.event.chart(df.test, c("study.entry.date", "first.sae.date",
"last.visit.date"),
order.var = "study.entry.date", sample.n = 100)

It's basic, but serves my needs for now!
--Erik
